_comment: FROZEN. E2E-SPEC v1.0 s13.10 (the section GATE1 Addendum A1 calls s13.9). The context/labels/traffic/kek blocks are P4-proposal values RATIFIED BYTE FOR BYTE by Security and MUST NOT be regenerated; the aead/negative/tamper/crossDirection blocks were specified and computed by Security in A1. Asserted by tests/kdf-vectors.test.mjs (web+SW) and by E2eKdfVectorsTest (android) against this same file.
_authority: GATE1.md "Addendum A1 — KDF/AEAD layout: AMENDED" — 2026-09-17T22:34Z, signed by the Gate 1 security signer.

tagRanges.reserved: every other value — a new tagged structure allocates a NEW range, it never reuses one

noncePrefixes._comment: Vector E — GATE1 Addendum A2 (RATIFIED A, 2026-09-17T15:50Z). The 4-byte nonce prefix is DERIVED from SK and pairContext, exactly as TLS 1.3 derives its record IV (RFC 8446 s5.3) and never transmits it. It replaces the word 'random' in A1's nonce line, which described a value the frozen frame has no field to carry. Same context and sessionKeyHex as the blocks above; computed by Security in an independent HKDF implementation. L = 4 and 'expand 32 then truncate to 4' are the same bytes, but implementations SHOULD request L = 4 so the intent is not mistaken for a truncated key.
noncePrefixes._warning: The prefix contributes ZERO nonce-uniqueness. A2 withdraws A1's 'defence in depth against a state-restore bug' rationale: the prefix is a deterministic function of SK and pairEpoch, so within one epoch a restore reproduces it exactly. A1's persist-before-emit / fail-closed counter rule is the SOLE control against nonce reuse. It MUST also never be persisted — re-derive it on every session construction.

negativeH._comment: Vector H. np2c MUST NOT equal nc2p, and neither may be all-zero. A2's derivation cannot produce equal prefixes for distinct labels; an implementation that fed the same label twice would, and that is a one-character typo.

ctxWire._comment: Vector I — GATE1 Addendum A3 (RATIFIED A AMENDED, 2026-09-17T23:41Z). pairContext is derived from the ctx object carried on ACCEPT_PAIRING / PAIRING_ACTIVE / PAIR_STATE.e2e PLUS the receiver's OWN session userId. userId is deliberately NOT transmitted: each side uses its own authenticated identity and a mismatch fails closed, where transmitting it would let the relay propose an identity and the derivation would then agree with the relay instead of with the session. Computed by Security in an independent HKDF/GCM implementation (security/PROJECTS/computercaller/e2e/a3-vectors-verify.mjs).
ctxWire._assertion: wire ctx + local userId == the frozen local context, byte for byte. I.1's contextBytesHex is identical to this file's own contextBytesHex, and A2 vector F's ciphertext opens under the key and prefix derived from the wire form.

positiveI1.pairEpochNote: DECIMAL STRING, never a JSON number: JSON.parse yields a double and A1 forbids pairEpoch rounding above 2^53. Receivers MUST parse with BigInt and reject anything not matching ^(0|[1-9][0-9]{0,19})$ or exceeding 2^64-1 — no Number(), no leading zeros, no sign, no whitespace.

negativeI2EpochDrift._comment: The A3-M2 replay case. A relay that replays an old ACCEPT_PAIRING block re-installs a superseded SK under its old epoch, and A2's per-(kid,direction) counter restarts at 0 against a key-and-prefix pair that has already sealed frames — GCM nonce reuse. Each computer-side device MUST persist a floor lastPairEpoch[(userId, phoneDeviceId)], write it BEFORE the derived keys are used, and refuse any ctx.pairEpoch <= floor.

negativeI3UserIdDrift._comment: Proves the UN-transmitted field is load-bearing: one character of local session identity yields total key divergence. This is the fail-closed behaviour A3 intends, pinned by a vector instead of by intent.

negativeI4Parser._comment: All of these MUST throw/refuse at ctx ingest, never coerce. A3-M3: a receiver MUST refuse a block whose ctx.peerDeviceId is not its own deviceId and — wherever it independently knows the value — whose ctx.pairingId differs from the pairingId it is party to. A3-M4: a mode=1 block arriving with NO ctx MUST be refused, never derived-from-local, because deriving from a locally guessed context is precisely the silent divergence A3 exists to kill and would let a stripping relay force both sides into a guess.
negativeI4Parser.badPairEpochNote: 42 is the JSON NUMBER 42, not the string; absent is covered by missingPairEpoch below.
negativeI4Parser.oversizeNote: A1's encode-time throw, re-asserted on the DECODE side: a 256-byte id arriving from the wire must be refused, not truncated to len & 0xff.

canonicalPeer._comment: Vector J — GATE1 Addendum A4 (RATIFIED (1) AMENDED, 2026-09-17T20:58Z). A4 supersedes A3-M3 IN FULL. There is ONE ctx, ONE pairContext, ONE traffic-key set and ONE nonce-prefix pair per pairing, shared by every recipient; ctx.peerDeviceId is the CANONICAL PEER — the byte-wise lexicographically lowest wraps[].deviceId, compared as raw UTF-8 bytes — not the receiver. Per-recipient separation lives where it already belonged: the KEK, which binds the recipient's own static key on top of the shared context. Computed by Security in an independent clean-room HKDF/GCM implementation (security/PROJECTS/computercaller/e2e/a4-vectors-verify.mjs), importing nothing from lib/e2e/kdf.mjs. Fixtures continue A3's, so J composes with E-H and I instead of standing apart.
canonicalPeer._assertion: Two recipients, one ctx: both derive identical traffic keys and prefixes, ONE broadcast ciphertext opens for BOTH, and their KEKs still differ. J.3 proves A4 rekeys nothing already shipped — its steered k_p2c is byte-identical to vector I.1's frozen phoneToComputerKeyHex, so the single-recipient path is unchanged.
canonicalPeer._canonicalSetNote: The canonical set is wraps[].deviceId, NOT recipKeys[]. recipKeys[] is the FULL static key set of the pairing — SEC1 public keys, and it INCLUDES THE PHONE (lib/e2eBlock-core.js:152-155); a lowest-of-recipKeys[] is neither a deviceId nor a recipient-only set. wraps[].deviceId is bounded 1..128 chars and already proven duplicate-free (lib/e2eBlock-core.js:169-173), and that uniqueness is what makes lowest a TOTAL order with no tie to break.
canonicalPeer.wrapsOrderNote: Deliberately ordered so the canonical lowest is NOT first in array order: an implementation that returned wraps[0] would pass a same-order fixture. Selection is order-independent, so a relay that re-orders wraps[] without editing it cannot steer the derivation.

positiveJ1bBroadcast._comment: The property device-scoped ctx (resolution (2)) would destroy. Sealed phone data frames are ONE ciphertext broadcast byte-identically to every listener (server.js broadcastToListeners(room, msg, perSocket = null); the per-socket builder exists ONLY for PAIR_STATE). Under a per-recipient key set that single frame would open for exactly one recipient and present the other with a GCM tag failure indistinguishable from a network fault — a silent, permanent, unattributable half-break.
positiveJ1bBroadcast.aadNote: EMPTY AAD, deliberately: J fixes it so this vector stands alone and does not re-pin A2's frame header.

positiveJ1cKeks._comment: Where per-recipient separation actually lives: kekInfo = cc-e2e-v1/kek || pairContext || 0x15 u8(65) K_i. Same ctx, different static key, different KEK — so one shared traffic-key set costs no per-recipient wrap separation. Static keys from fixed P-256 scalars 1 and 2.

negativeJ2PairingId._comment: A3-M3(a), unchanged by A4. Refused BEFORE any derivation, fail-closed. Checked only where the receiver independently knows the value: passing ctx.pairingId back as its own expectation is a check that CANNOT FAIL, which is worse than no check because it reads like one that can.

negativeJ3SteeredPeer._comment: A3-M3(c), re-scoped. Same pairing, ctx.peerDeviceId forced to the NON-canonical dev-web-01. A receiver holding wraps[] MUST refuse this BEFORE deriving. A receiver that does NOT hold the set (the extension service worker, via PAIR_STATE, which carries only its own wrap) MUST NOT attempt this check and MUST NOT substitute its own deviceId — for it, the binding check is the cryptographic one: its wrap opens under KEK(ctx, its own static key).
negativeJ3SteeredPeer.singleRecipientInvarianceNote: SINGLE-RECIPIENT INVARIANCE, the proof that A4 rekeys nothing already shipped: this phoneToComputerKeyHex is BYTE-IDENTICAL to vector I.1's traffic phoneToComputerKeyHex. For a one-recipient pairing the canonical lowest IS that recipient, so tag 0x13 keeps its existing encoding (one id, u8-length-prefixed, no count byte, no list) and the context bytes are byte-identical to what ships today. Two independent clean-room implementations agree on it. A4 adds no row to E-H or I and forces no re-pair.
negativeJ3SteeredPeer.residualRiskNote: A relay that REWRITES wraps[].deviceId (renaming, not re-keying) can move the canonical peer and desynchronise derivation. DENIAL OF SERVICE ONLY: the relay holds no SK, gains no plaintext, and every recipient fails closed on frame one. Not a downgrade, not key confusion. Accepted, with the reasoning recorded so it is not rediscovered as a finding.

negativeJ4NonMember._comment: A3-M3(b), the cryptographic membership check — and the SW lane's binding one. A device whose static key comes from scalar 3 has no wraps[] entry addressed to it; a wrap spliced from another recipient does not open under its KEK. Either condition refuses, fail-closed, NO plaintext fallback and NO degrade to counts-only. A4-M3: unwrap failure is a PAIRING ABORT. s13.2 row 2's SW-absent counts-only badges covers a recipient that never had a key; it does NOT cover one whose wrap failed to open, which is a tampered or mismatched pairing.

negativeJ5PreA4Regression._comment: The pre-A4 check (ctx.peerDeviceId !== own deviceId -> refuse) applied to J.1 REFUSES dev-web-01 while ADMITTING dev-ext-02 — at most one recipient per pairing. Verified against 46e3084's lib/e2e/kdf.mjs, which threw ctx.peerDeviceId-is-not-this-device for dev-web-01. This assertion MUST fail before A4-M1 and pass after, otherwise the fix is unpinned.

canonicalPeer.assertionSplitNote: What makes J cross-implementation rather than two copies of one belief: P4 asserts J.1 + J.3's canonical selection through its ENCODE path (it builds wraps[] and picks the peer); P2 asserts J.1/J.1b/J.1c/J.3/J.5 through its DECODE path with the full wraps[]; P3 asserts J.1/J.1b/J.4 through the PAIR_STATE path WITHOUT the deviceId set, proving A3-M3(c) is correctly skipped there and (b) correctly binds.
canonicalPeer.sasNote: s13.3 stays FROZEN — deviceIds are NOT added to the SAS. pairingId (the salt) + pairEpoch + the full static key set K_1..K_n already cover everything the canonical-peer choice can affect: pairingId and pairEpoch are SAS-visible, and phoneDeviceId/peerDeviceId are key-binding (editing either yields universal authentication failure on frame one — a property A4 STRENGTHENS, since one shared key set means a tampered canonical peer breaks EVERY recipient identically and loudly). Adding deviceIds would re-freeze s13.3 for zero security property and would make the user-facing digits depend on relay-mutable NON-KEY metadata, converting a rename from both-sides-fail-loudly into the-digits-also-disagree — teaching users to dismiss mismatches.

canonicalPeerByteOrder._comment: Vector K — GATE1 'Addendum A4 — vector K: COUNTERSIGNED', 2026-09-17T19:07:20Z, authored and independently recomputed by Security in a clean room (security/PROJECTS/computercaller/e2e/a4-vector-k-verify.mjs, importing nothing from lib/e2e/kdf.mjs). Frozen VERBATIM. Fixtures are vector J's and UNCHANGED (SK a0a1..bebf, pairingId/salt pair-7f3a9c21, phoneDeviceId dev-phone-01, pairEpoch 42, LOCAL userId user-0191aa, labels cc-e2e-v1/{p2c,c2p,np2c,nc2p}); only wraps[].deviceId differs, so K isolates the canonical-ORDER rule from everything else.
canonicalPeerByteOrder._whyJIsNotEnough: Vector J's deviceIds are pure ASCII, where unsigned UTF-8 byte order, SIGNED byte order and UTF-16 code-unit order all AGREE. J therefore cannot catch a wrong comparator at all. K is the fixture where they disagree. P4 hit exactly this on Android at 86aed97.
canonicalPeerByteOrder._whyTwoVectors: ONE two-id vector cannot pin both bugs, and Security's countersign is explicit that K1 alone does NOT satisfy the requirement. Signed-vs-unsigned byte order diverges only when the first differing byte is ASCII vs non-ASCII; UTF-16-vs-code-point order diverges only when the first differing CHARACTER is BMP>=U+E000 vs supplementary. Those conditions are MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE at the same position — a supplementary lead byte is F0..F4 and a BMP>=E000 lead byte is EE/EF, both non-ASCII, so signed and unsigned agree there. On K1's pair a signed-Byte Kotlin implementation gives the CORRECT answer and would PASS; K2 is what catches it.
canonicalPeerByteOrder._correctionToAddendum2: Ken's Addendum 2 stated that U+10000 (F0 90 80 80) sorts BELOW U+FFFD (EF BF BD) under unsigned UTF-8 byte order. Security's countersign rules that INVERTED and binding: UTF-8 unsigned byte order is identical to Unicode code-point order, 0xEF < 0xF0, so U+FFFD sorts BELOW U+10000 and is the canonical peer. The inverted direction is the UTF-16 answer (D800 < FFFD) — precisely the WRONG answer the vector exists to catch, so freezing it would have pinned the bug instead of the rule. A4-R2's RULE is unchanged; only Addendum 2's illustrative direction was wrong.
canonicalPeerByteOrder._rule: canonicalPeerDeviceId(wraps) MUST compare new TextEncoder().encode(id) (Uint8Array, unsigned by construction) element-wise, shorter-is-lower on a common prefix. It MUST NOT use JS string <, Array.prototype.sort on strings, Kotlin String.minOrNull()/compareTo, or any signed-Byte comparison.

sharedFixture.sessionKeyRef: traffic.sessionKeyHex (a0a1..bebf) — the same SK as E-H, I and J

K1._comment: Catches UTF-16 code-unit order — Kotlin String.minOrNull(), JS string <. U+FFFD is one code unit FFFD; U+10000 is the surrogate pair D800 DC00, and D800 < FFFD, so UTF-16 order picks the WRONG id.

negativeK1_2Utf16Pick._comment: The id a UTF-16-ordering implementation would choose. The page lane, which holds wraps[], MUST REFUSE this ctx — and the derived key is included to show the failure is silent without that refusal: the derivation SUCCEEDS, it is simply a key nobody else holds.

K1_3SignedIsVacuous._comment: Signed byte order picks id A on this pair — the CORRECT id — so K1 cannot detect a signed-Byte implementation. Recorded explicitly so nobody mistakes K1 for full coverage. This is exactly why K2 exists.

K2._comment: Catches SIGNED byte comparison — Kotlin Byte, Java byte. 0x7A is +122 and 0xF0 is -16, so a signed comparison picks the WRONG id while unsigned correctly picks the ASCII one.

negativeK2_3SignedPick._comment: The id a signed-Byte implementation would choose (0xF0 -> -16 < 0x7A -> 122). Page lane MUST REFUSE. Note the ctx and key are byte-identical to K1.2's, because both wrong comparators land on the same supplementary id — which is why the two vectors share a negative and still pin different bugs.

K2_2Utf16IsVacuous._comment: UTF-16 order picks id A on this pair — the CORRECT id — so K2 cannot detect a UTF-16-ordering implementation. That is why K1 exists. Together K1 and K2 leave no wrong comparator that passes both.

K4LaneScope._comment: Unchanged from A4. Clause (c) — the canonical-peer check — is evaluated ONLY where the receiver holds wraps[] (the page lane, via ACCEPT_PAIRING / PAIRING_ACTIVE). The SW lane (PAIR_STATE, singular wrap) skips (c) and MUST NOT substitute its own deviceId; its cryptographic anchor remains clause (b) — its own wrap opens under KEK(ctx, its own static key).
K4LaneScope.swLaneAnchor: clause (b): own wrap opens under KEK(ctx, own static key)

comparatorTruthTable._comment: Exactly one column is correct for BOTH rows, so no single wrong comparator satisfies the whole block and no subset of it passes by luck.

aead._comment: Vector A and the negative cases B/C/D were specified and computed by Security in Addendum A1. A is verified against traffic.phoneToComputerKeyHex above.

vectorA.paddedPlaintextNote: s13.4 padded "hi": be32(2) || "hi" || 0x00*58, the 64-byte bucket. Pad FIRST, then seal.

vectorF._comment: Vector F — A2. The SAME frame as vector A, so the two differ in exactly ONE input (the nonce prefix) and any divergence localises immediately. A's prefix is an explicit input (the 'given a prefix, seal correctly' test and it stays as-is); F's is DERIVED, so it is the 'derive the prefix correctly' test.

vectorG._comment: Vector G — A2. The reverse direction, proving the direction byte, the c2p key and the c2p prefix all move TOGETHER. An implementation that flipped the AAD byte but kept the p2c key (or the p2c prefix) passes F and fails only here.

negativeOversizeIds._comment: A1 (4): u8 is RATIFIED over u16, but the cap MUST be enforced, not assumed. Each of these MUST THROW at encode on every platform. A test that only proves the happy path does not prove the cap is enforced.

tamper._comment: Flip the AAD direction byte 0x01(p2c) -> 0x02(c2p) and the GCM tag check MUST fail. Proves the AAD is actually passed and not dropped: a silently-ignored AAD is indistinguishable from a working one on the happy path.

crossDirection._comment: k_c2p MUST NOT open vector A. This is what makes a reflected frame inert (A1 (2)).

vectorL._comment: Vector L - GATE1 Addendum FT-A1, frozen 2026-09-18. Specified and computed by Security in `ft-a1-vector-l-verify.mjs` (clean-room, node:crypto only, 14/14 PASS); the copy in tools/ is byte-identical to the ledger original. Transcribed here by E2E-P1.3 (b) because the source is a LEDGER file that a gate run cannot read. NOTHING WAS ADJUSTED to make it agree with the repo: every value below is the verifier's output, and tests/kdf-vectors.test.mjs re-derives all of it through lib/e2e/* - a mismatch is a FINDING, not a fixture to repair.
vectorL._whatItPins: The FILE_OFFER envelope hint `ft:{id,size}` lives OUTSIDE the AAD. The whole security argument rests on two facts this vector makes checkable: (1) tampering with the hint leaves the ciphertext BYTE-IDENTICAL (L2), so the AEAD cannot and must not be asked to defend it; (2) the receiver's post-unseal compare against the SEALED body is what actually defends it. A relay can make a transfer fail - which it can always do by dropping - and cannot make one proceed on a false size.
vectorL._selfContainedContext: Unlike vectors A/F/G, L does NOT use the file's top-level `context`. It carries its own fixtures because Security generated it under its own pairing, and re-keying it to the shared context would be exactly the 'adjustment' the transcription forbids.
vectorL.keySource: HKDF(cc-e2e-v1/p2c) over this vector's OWN contextBytesHex - DERIVED, not an input
vectorL.aadNote: The frozen five-field layout, unchanged. The hint contributes NOTHING to it - that absence is the vector.
vectorL.paddedPlaintextNote: s13.4: 210 B + 4 B length prefix = 214 -> the 256 B bucket. FILE_OFFER is NOT *_CHUNK, so it pads.
vectorL.hintNote: FT-A1 A-1: `ft:{id,size}`, not `ft:{size}`. Without `id` neither the SW nor the relay can author a FILE_FAILED and the relay has nothing to key a meter on. `id` is 16 random bytes with zero semantic content.

L2_relayLowersHint.ciphertextNote: BYTE-IDENTICAL to L1: the hint is outside the AAD, so the AEAD sees no change

L3_hintStripped.relayGateNote: FT-A1 A-2: fail CLOSED, or every sender bypasses tier+quota by omitting one field

L4_counterfactualAadBound.note: The REJECTED design: ft.size moved INTO the AAD under tag 0x26. It works - the tampered hint fails the GCM tag - and it is rejected anyway, because it forks the frozen aad() layout for one frame type and buys nothing L2 does not already buy. Frozen here so the rejection stays checkable rather than remembered. 0x26 is NOT a ratified allocation.

L5_lyingSender.note: THE HOLE. Both values are lies told by the SAME party - the one the quota is charged to - so both checks pass and the sender then streams 700 MiB. Cost charged: 1 KiB. Repeatable.
L5_lyingSender.closedBy: FT-A1 A-3/A-4 + A1.1 metering: the relay meters ACTUAL FILE_CHUNK WIRE bytes per (room, ft.id) and aborts on overrun. Chunks are padding-exempt, so the count is exact and free.
